subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT RESOLUTION

speechtext:
Resolved that it is expedient to amend the Excise Tax Act to provide that, effective January 1, 1967, the rate of the consumption or sales tax imposed under section 30 of the said act be increased from 8 per cent to 9 per cent with respect to all goods subject to the said tax, except articles enumerated in schedule V of the said act and building materials that were exempt from the said tax immediately prior to June 14, 1963.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last night when the house adjourned, I was commenting the resolution providing for a 1 per cent increase of the indirect federal tax. In fact, the resolution mentions that the tax is increased from 8 to 9 per cent. However, we know full well that it is not an 8 per cent tax but an 11 per cent tax. We are dealing with an 11 per cent indirect sales tax, hidden in the cost price, and it is being raised to 12 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, recently the minister has been trying, at least according to his speeches, to check inflation, to check rising costs and the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. Still, through these increases in hidden taxes, the minister is the one who contributes the most to inflation and the devaluation of the Canadian dollar.
Yesterday, I explained that a 1 per cent increase in the federal sales tax could lead to a 4 per cent increase in the cost of living, because, as we know, the provincial sales tax of 6 per cent, for instance, applies to the total cost price, including the 11 per cent and, from here on, the 12 per cent. Consequently, when the total cost price of the manufacturer goes up by 1 per cent, the wholesaler, the retailer and all the middlemen will take their percentage oft that increase. I showed yesterday, with figures, how an article costing $10 would sell for far more today, due to the increase in 23033-827
Ways and Means
the sales tax, from the wholesaler to the consumer through the retailer and other middlemen. I added that we would witness, not a 1 per cent increase in prices but rather a 2 per cent increase.
Mr. Chairman, I say therefore to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) that, in times such as these, where prices are skyrocketing, and everyone complains continuously of the rising cost of living, the move he is now contemplating will lead to even greater inflation than any other decision did in the last year, whether they concerned increases in salaries, or anything else.
Mr. Chairman, I do not hesitate to say that the Minister of Finance is the first to do the opposite of what he preaches in his speeches. Even though he advocates price stability, he is the first to increase inflation by raising taxes as he is doing today.
In my opinion, there is another way to finance old age security pensions without increasing the sales tax. We did not complain, or at least, I did not, about the first resolution designed to provide part of the funds required to pay the $30 old age pension supplement to needy persons, because in that case, the maximum old age security tax on the personal taxable income was increased from $120 to $240, which meant that people with higher income were being taxed more while those in the lower income groups were not. That is why I did not object to that first resolution.
As for the second one designed to increase the sales tax by 1 per cent, I feel that such a decision will have repercussions on the whole economy and all the more as everything is on the increase nowadays.
One can read on the first page of today's La Presse that there will soon be a general increase in Quebec Hydro rates, when electricity rates were not supposed to increase but rather to decrease following the nationalization of Quebec power companies. However, hardly two years later, there is a general increase in electricity rates in Quebec. The construction of power stations is said to be costly. It is because the Minister of Finance imposed all those new taxes that all prices are going up, in the construction field as well. As a matter of fact, who pays for that, if not the small consumer, the small wage-earner who is constantly thrown off balance by the increased cost of living, inflation and the erosion of the Canadian dollar?
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say to the Minister of Finance that even though he

February 15, 1967
Ways and Means
makes eloquent speeches against inflation which presently prevails in Canada, he is the first person to blame because of his tax increases, and I vigorously object to this new increase which will create even more confusion and be the cause of more economic crises in Canada.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would feel remiss if I failed to speak to this resolution, because it strikes at the very heart of the Canadian people, I should like to ask the minister the reason for these tax increases, the valuation of Canadian dollar and the dissatisfaction all over Canada? The unions are dissatisfied as exemplified by strikes occurring throughout the country. Surely, Mr. Chairman, that is food for thought.
If we take a look at the economy of our country, then I submit to the hon. minister that it is unbalanced. Our economy is not balanced. And, as we go on applying the present system, we go on off-setting the economy, causing Canadians to be dissatisfied and making it more difficult for them to earn a living. Moreover a certain group of people are living off the fat of the land, taking advantage of the fruit and labour of other people; the system is fine for these individuals who succeed in monopolizing all interests and who keep all the profits to themselves. But this group is a minority in our society.
An important part of our population is happy today, Mr. Chairman, that its purchasing power has been increased by about $30 per month, or $1 a day. I am referring to the old people. For that, I extend my congratulations to the government and to all who forced the government to consider the essential needs of a small part of the Canadian people who are without other income.
It is something, Mr. Chairman, I realize it. It is better than nothing. And that is why I say "well done" to the government and to those who have helped in obtaining this increase of $30 per month for our senior citizens who well deserve a softer life in their declining years for. having gone through life financially harassed by a tax system that is unfair, inhuman, completely off kilter, inefficient and without any relation whatever with the financial facts of our national production, of our worthy population ever eager to do its best.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, the old people receive a guaranteed minimum income of $105 per month, and they can start to live properly.

This is cause for rejoicing and calls for congratulations for the government that passed this measure. It was high time.
What is regrettable, Mr. Chairman, is the attitude of the government particularly of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General of Canada (Mr. Sharp) on the means required to raise the monies necessary to meet this additional guaranteed income of $30 per month for our older citizens. I may be blamed for repeating the same thing over again but it is due to the fact that the Minister of Finance and Receiver General of Canada always repeats the same gestures.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
And when the minister needs money to administer the business of the country, he always turns hurriedly towards the small wage earners, toward the people to get it. You asked for a $30 a month increase, here in the bill.
And everybody finds that normal. Well-known newspapermen, editors, leading newspapers repeat that wonderful sentence "The people ask for bonuses, the minister grants them, asking them at the same time to foot the bill". And that results in a tax increase, and the people bow to that request and accept that inevitable solution. And the minister is the winner. He might have left the people with the impression that all the increases, all the bonuses granted to the poor subjects of the realm require a tax increase, so that the people say in the long run that what the government gives with one hand, it takes back with the other, even twice as much, according to established practices.
The government can no longer balance its yearly budget. Every year, it shows deficits and the more it taxes, the more it has to borrow in order to make both ends meet. And the people are paying more and more taxes in this country, more and more interest on debts that are forever accumulating.
And yet, it is being said that Canada is a prosperous country. It is the most prosperous country in the world, next to the United States, our neighbour country. If our country is prosperous, Mr. Chairman, how is it that it cannot make both ends meet, that it cannot finance at a profit, why is there always a deficit? When someone is prosperous, he usually can make both ends meet every year.
If there is prosperity in Canada, Mr. Chairman, where is it? Can we see or touch that prosperity? And where do we get the money required to finance the needs of the government?
February 15. 1967

No, Mr. Chairman, the only way we have of financing the current needs of the government, is to levy taxes, particularly on small incomes, on the purchasing power, on consumption, on small wage-earners, even on the under-fed.
In the bill before us we are being asked to add a further 1 per cent to the consumption tax. The sales tax will be increased to 12 per cent from 11 per cent. That is all there is to it. To summarize this whole transaction, if more purchasing power is given, approximately $30 more per month to our senior citizens, it must come out of the purchasing power of all other citizens in Canada. The purchasing power is increased on both sides, but it is lowered elsewhere. Thus the whole Canadian population is worse off than before.
Indeed, what this involves is the setting-up of a costly system to administer this $30-per-month guaranteed income supplement to people over 68 years of age. When we add about $280 million worth of purchasing power for our senior citizens, that same amount, plus the tremendous administrative costs, come out of the pockets of all other Canadian citizens.
The situation in which people, in general, find themselves is, or will be, worse than before. And who profits by this financing method of our government, of this method of taxation of our government?
Do you want to know who always benefits from the perpetual abuse of the purchasing power of the low income of the Canadian people?
Do you want to know how prosperous part of our population really is, when the rest suffer so much hardship and poverty?
My information comes from no less a source than our national statistics, the statistics of the Minister of Finance which could have shown him where to levy taxes, if he cannot find money elsewhere.
In 1966, Mr. Chairman, Canadian production reached the $56 billion mark but consumption only reached $38 billion. Therefore there was a surplus in Canada of $18 billion, and yet the minister does not know where to find the $280 million he needs.
The common people in Canada, the small tradesmen or the small manufacturers bene-fitted to the extent of $38 billion only while the other $18 billion went to a few large financial institutions.
Are those $18 billion which went-into the coffers of a small group of prosperous companies and individuals in Canada so sacred that 23033-827i
Ways and Means
this small amount of $280 million could not come out of this sum. Those $280 millions must come out of the limited purchasing power of the poor people instead of the $18 billion surplus earned by a few privileged individuals and companies in Canada.
Who governs in Canada? Are we living in a democracy elected by the people, for the people? Are we a plutocracy elected by financiers, by banks and company directors only? Whom does the Minister of Finance represent? Is he the representative of the whole people or of the rich, the powerful, the scholars only? When he needs $280 million for the administration of his department, he always spares the "big-earners" who capitalized $18 billion in 1966, and he squeezes the low wage-earners whose deficits and debts increase every year.
That is the topsy-turvy way in which the Department of Finance works, Mr. Chairman. The purchasing power of the low income groups is curtailed to increase the capitalization yield of millionaires.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we are not against millionaires, we are not against capitalization but, under the present system, if other means or sources of revenues cannot be found to obtain capital, the small wage-earner should not always be the one to be overtaxed and the protection of large corporations with billions of dollars hidden in their reserves should cease. Big businesses are allowed to hide all kinds of reserves and the people suffer hardship as a result. When new taxes or new credit restrictions are imposed, low income groups are always the ones who suffer, who pay and who are taxed.
The present sheep-shearing system, Mr. Chairman, is designed to fatten the hogs. Is there prosperity in Canada when 2,400,000 small wage-earners cannot support their families because of their low income or are not making enough money to even pay income tax? Yet the cost of living goes up for them through a taxation system which is crushing low income groups for the benefit of big businesses.
How long will this go on, Mr. Chairman? When will those who are getting fat on crumbs falling off the table of the Canadian poor be satisfied?
Mr. Chairman, for over three years now we have repeatedly asked the Minister of Finance to change his taxation methods. He does not seem to know what to do, so he

February 15, 1967
Ways and Means
carries on as heretofore. Is that all he can do, carry on as heretofore? It may be true that man is descended from the monkey, but judging from the minister's actions, some men may not have descended yet.
Mr. Chairman, Canada can no longer be administered as in the past. The past is gone. The past has done its work. The future is at our door-step now and the people to-day do not want yesterday's methods. A nation producing affluence will no longer be content to live in poverty, misery, need and insecurity.
Each year, compared with those citizens who deny themselves the necessities of life, others accumulate some 18 billion in capital. Is this what we call economic balance? Is this the result of what we call a sound administration? Is that what is called good currency circulation? Is that what is called equity among the different members of the same society, those who suffer and those who enjoy life, those who are increasingly suffering besides those with ever-increasing enjoyment and assets?
The proper solution to present conditions has been suggested. Drawers are full of data which are gathering dust and are not taken into consideration, because the situation is deemed satisfactory. Those who have provided slush funds must be repaid. This is the secret of the minister's unconcern before the confusion of the people, the deficit of the government and a $18 billion capitalization of a few individuals and private companies.
The minister has a free hand. Now that he is making up the supplementary guaranteed income of $30 per month with taxes levied on the small wage-earner, with increases of the cost of living and price increases on goods, he expects that the people will no longer ask him for any free services. But he must not rely so soon on his success. The old people are not the only ones who need a guaranteed income for a strict vital minimum, for the right of living in Canada.
This is only the beginning. The minister would do better to ascertain where to raise revenues and levy taxes. He should immediately collect them from the $18 billion of annual capitalization rather than from the low income of small wage-earners who must support their family on a salary insufficient even for an unmarried person, a salary which they do not And satisfactory, a salary which is not sufficient to provide for their normal needs.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, the people will never be satisfied as long as family allowances are not

increased, as long as family allowances are not adjusted according to the cost of living and as long as a salary has not been granted to students, to mothers, in short to all those who need it, in Canada.
In any case, what we need in Canada, Mr. Chairman, is consumers. We have them, but they do not have money to purchase products. The purchasing power is reduced by an increase in taxes, an increase in salaries, an increase in interests on capital. The purchasing power is reduced and so is the value of the Canadian dollar. Canadians have less and less purchasing power. The more Canadians produce, the less money they have to purchase those products.
That situation is not normal, Mr. Chairman.
This situation should be remedied. In such circumstances, one should take the advice of those who suggest solutions. If the minister cannot find better solutions, than those suggested to him, he should at least be gracious enough to accept the ones that are offered. In passing, I should like to tell the hon. minister that we do not seek power, but solutions. If the solutions proposed by the minister are not valid socially and do not satisfy the needs of the people, he should change his way of proceeding. If he cannot find other practical ways of stabilizing the national economy and balancing the budget of every family and individual, let him accept the solutions of those who have found some. Those who offer solutions to the minister are not irresponsible people. The problems have been studied for years, and the minister has not been able to find better solutions for them; he should at least accept those that are offered to him. One fine day he will see that he is able to bring about a satisfactory settlement of the unbalanced economic situation that we are experiencing at the present time.
We even want this guaranteed income for those without personal income to be taken from the fiscal and administrative privileges that are enjoyed by large companies and from people who are granted all kinds of tax reductions because their income tax is not deducted at the source.
We have nothing against the people whose income tax is not deducted at the source. We wish everybody could be like that. Once again, Mr. Chairman, if another formula cannot be found besides taxing at the source to get revenue, we should know at least that those who have money, those who make money, those who have capital, those who
February 15, 1987

have hidden reserves, those who benefit from the present system are also taxed.
With all the people, we want that guaranteed minimum income to come out of the capitalization of $18 billion of some people and companies which are the only ones to know prosperity in Canada, next to the governments which accumulate deficits each year, the large families, the many people who are in debt up to their ears, who cannot balance their budget, and much less pay their taxes.
As far as the small manufacturers and businessmen are concerned, they will soon have to give up, because they are so heavily taxed that they cannot make enough money to pay their taxes. They are unable to expand, to increase their production. They cannot do it because they need new capital and the government will get it through its taxes.
The small manufacturers and businessmen are on the brink of bankruptcy, not to mention those who go bankrupt. There will be a great number of business failures within a few months. As a matter of fact, a large number of small businesses, stores and industries are unable to expand, to balance their budget, to pay their provincial, municipal and school taxes or even their federal taxes.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, we should be most concerned. The situation is serious. If the free enterprise system is to be maintained and helped, if we do not want to be led into the arms of socialism, into the arms of absolute communism, into state socialism which controls and plans everything and where the state spends all the taxpayers' money for them, we must be concerned about the present situation, we must be practical and bring in legislation to balance the Canadian economy. In every sphere of society, in industry in business, in private families, there is a general lack of balance, and that is why there is cause for dissatisfaction across the country.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I shall say this to the minister: It is urgent that he open his eyes and ears and consider the deplorable state of our economy. Reforms must be implemented and they are badly needed because the people of Canada cannot and do not want to wait any longer. Families in need of food cannot wait any longer for food on credit because they have been using credit long enough and their credit rating is now nil. They cannot get any more credit. They must have money, "cash money", and it is our job to see to it that families and institutions are
Ways and Means
able to administer their own affairs, take advantage of the surplus of goods in Canada, even though one quarter or one third of the population are unemployed or non productive for some reason or other, receiving unemployment insurance or social welfare benefits. If our system enabled us to have a balanced economy, all those people would be working and this would increase productivity which would result in a better economy for Canada; at present they cannot even purchase goods since they do not have the money necessary to provide for their needs.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, everyone in the house must have wondered at the philosophy of the government in imposing two taxes on the Canadian public for the purpose, as the minister said, of balancing the budget as a result of the granting of the old age supplementary benefit. There must have been surprise and perhaps even shock when the Minister of National Health and Welfare said that we will have to provide all Canadians with at least a minimum standard of living. It is possible that many people in the Liberal party disagreed with that statement and I think one of them must have been the Minister of Finance. When he introduced the increase in the old age security payment he did not take the opportunity to eliminate the ceiling, something which has been recommended on many occasions and would have brought about the same result as raising the limitation on contributions from $120 to $240. Actually the minister has protected the upper level of taxpayers and therefore he has done exactly the reverse of what the Minister of National Health and Welfare intended in trying to establish a minimum income base. Certainly the sales tax affects all Canadians but it is highly detrimental to people with low incomes. The minister has said that such things as building materials will be exempted from this tax.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT RESOLUTION
speechtext: Food and rent, too.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Food and rent were exempted before, so we are getting into a different field. Prior to 1963, of course, there were taxes applied on building materials, but we decided we were not going to increase the cost of building materials because the opportunity for house building in the low income groups has practically been eliminated. It is a fact that the poor people in every community in Canada are unable even to paint their houses

February 15, 1967
Ways and Means
let alone repair them because of this tax on building materials.
I asked one of my colleagues if I would be correct in assuming that an increase in the sales tax of 1 per cent would probably increase the cost of living by 2 per cent. Last night the hon. member for Lapointe indicated that he believes the cost of living would be increased by 5 per cent. I assume, therefore, I would not be incorrect in suggesting that the cost of living would be increased by 2 per cent. I believe the minister had no right to slap the wrists of the poorer people, whom we have been unable to help, by adding to their difficulties through an increase in the sales tax which is not going to do what the minister implied it would do, that is, balance the old age security fund. In my opinion the fund could have been balanced if the minister had removed entirely the ceiling on contributions to the old age security fund made by those in the higher income brackets. These moneys would have gone directly into the fund. The results achieved when we increased the ceiling on payments into the fund from $90 to $120 indicate that if we had long ago entirely removed the ceiling, which only applies to the upper one-third of income taxpayers, sufficient money would have been provided for a considerable length of time.
I feel that the sales tax is extremely detrimental. I believe that the Liberal party should look at the situation because one minister is trying to raise the standard of living of our people to a reasonable level by setting a minimum income of $105 while at the same time another minister is counteracting that proposal. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has said that eventually there should be a guaranteed minimum annual income for all Canadians, and with that I agree. I believe it is time we took a look at the protection that is necessary for crippled children, for those who are mentally defective and others who are handicapped through no fault of their own. They should be provided with a decent standard of living.
But what have we done? Every person who has to buy clothes, which in Canada are a necessity of life, is to be charged an extra 1 per cent. However, the 1 per cent will be multiplied by the effect of provincial taxes, profits and so on. The increase will probably amount to 5 per cent or 10 per cent finally. These people are not able to buy automobiles or luxury goods and they will find the cost of their ordinary needs increased by reason of the increase in the sales tax.

I suggest that in some cases the cost of goods will be 100 per cent higher. I suggest there are many members on the government side who recognize the fact that the 1 per cent increase will be multiplied four or five times and will bring undue hardship to all their constituents who are hard-pressed now. The increase will tend to discourage many constituents who are finding it difficult to make ends meet. I was watching a television program the other night on which it was suggested that one family had a bill of $240 for drugs for one child who has a permanent disability. I believe we would not be true to ourselves if we were to increase the burden of this family by 5 per cent or 10 per cent. I suggest this is the effect a sales tax increase will have.

The individual with a low income is harder hit by educational taxes than by other taxes. I think the minister will agree that the sales tax on commodities that have to be purchased by individuals is normally added on at the manufacturing level and is multiplied by provincial taxes and the profit that is taken. Eventually the consumer has to pay all this. The minister has mentioned that food is exempted, and that is true. However, when you walk into a grocery store you find that many commodities which the poorest people in the nation have to buy are taxable. It has always surprised me that a necessary item like soap is taxed. Toilet paper, cleaning fluid and many other commodities are also taxed. The increase in the sales tax will apply to such items and will work great hardship on the people.

[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I suggest that the minister has been giving us a lecture. If the increase in the sales tax is a manifestation of his philosophy, perhaps the nation should be given this type of lecture. Perhaps we should be told to pay our way and to balance our budget. However, just because the minister is angry at the decision of some of his colleagues to provide a minimum supplementary benefit for needy old age pensioners, he should not tax those who are in desperate straits. This is particularly so in the case of the old age pensioners and those in the low income brackets.
I believe that the $155 million which will be added to the old age security fund may still not be enough to keep the fund stable, though I have never felt that it necessarily should be. I have always felt that most of the old age pensioners have worked hard during their lives, at times for as little as 25 cents an hour, and that our present gross national product has resulted from their earning power over the years. But because the cost of living is rising today, these people have been unable to prepare adequately for their retirement. If we are unable to work out some system to care for our elderly citizens through a fund to which they have contributed, then I think it is generally agreed by most Canadians, our gross national product being what it is, that some other means must be found to provide for them.
I believe that the application of this tax is wrong and that the minister will hurt those least able to pay it. In my area many people are applying for the disabled person's allowance, widow's allowance or mother's allowance, and they send me a list of their groceries with the prices they have to pay. Their budgets are very tight, and if the increase in the sales tax is applied to even half the items that they buy it will mean they will have to economize in the only way they can, on food. In this event the minister will to an extent be depriving these people of a commodity that is not even subject to the tax.
I suggest that most people will disagree with the minister's effort when he introduced this budget on December 19 to balance the old age security fund by collecting additional tax to help pay for the supplementary benefits. If we wanted the fund to be in a solvent position we would obviously have removed the $240 ceiling. This step would probably affect those in the $10,000 range who would be able to continue making payments to the fund above the amount of $240 and up to the
Ways and Means
maximum of their earning capacity. This would provide additional revenue to enable the minister to balance the fund. It is very difficult to say whether this would meet the entire cost. I have not looked up the figures to see how much we took out of the fund when we raised the levy from $90 to $120. Therefore I am only guessing that if we went beyond the $5,000 taxable level the fund would be balanced.
However, I suggest that the country is not necessarily interested in balancing the fund. I suggest that many members of the Liberal party who applauded so loudly when the minister introduced this measure will have to wrestle with their consciences when they come to vote for the 1 per cent increase in the excise tax raising it to 12 per cent. They know that it will have a detrimental effect on all those in their ridings in need of welfare who do not now receive the old age supplement. If these members are honest with themselves they will realize that this tax will apply to many of the consumer products these people require.
Other hon. members have mentioned an aspect which will probably appeal to some members much more. I refer to the effect this tax will have on the manufacturing processes in Canada which enable us to trade with other countries. Having talked to officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce about trade with other countries, I believe that an increase of even 1 or 2 per cent in the price of our commodities will make the difference between whether or not Canadian manufacturers will be able to export their goods.
So, Mr. Chairman, for many reasons I am prepared to oppose the introduction of the 1 per cent increase in the sales tax. I might say to the minister that had I been a member of the Ontario legislature when that government took the retrograde step of increasing the sales tax in that province, I would likewise have been happy to oppose such a step as being, in my opinion, not the type of tax that is either good for the economy or good for the low income earners.

Not only that, Mr. Chairman, but we are experiencing difficulty today in competing in the markets of the world. We are committing the folly of increasing our sales tax by 1 per cent, thus making it still more difficult for us to compete. In the first place, Mr. Chairman, how necessary is this tax increase? As I understand it, there is a fund, though the Minister of Finance does not seem to know where that fund is. speechtext:
1 thank the minister for that answer. This program is projected into the future. Some people in the old age group will not receive anything under the guaranteed income plan. Many will receive $1 or more up to $30 per month. The minister is taxing people who earn, say, $50 a month. People who have done a little work and have earned that much will be taxed $25 by the government. They will therefore obtain about $5 in guaranteed income.
It strikes me that somewhere there is unnecessary bookkeeping and bureaucracy. We are probably looking too far ahead. While nobody can predict exactly what future amounts of money will be required, I would have been happier had the minister used the $130 million and then said to the country, "We need more money; we shall have to impose a tax." This would have been a more common-sense approach, more fair to the old age pensioners. They would not have been reminded that a tax was imposed for them.
I can hear some old people saying, "It seems we must be reminded that we are causing increased taxes and raising the prices of goods everybody buys." The old people earned their money, money that some of them found hard to earn, when the dollar was worth one-third of today's dollar and their wages were less than one-fifth of today's wages. It would have been better had the minister or the government brought in a provision to pay something below $105 a month and utilized the Canada Assistance Plan for increases instead of adopting a plan offering up to $105 a month with a means test in conjunction with programs involving another means test administered by provincial governments. If the minister is as good at bookkeeping as he appears to be, why, especially in view of the deficits which have been mentioned, could he not have found other places to save this money instead of going into a field affecting everybody in this country?
To recapitulate, I say that raising the tax by 1 per cent will make competition more difficult. It will cost the people more money for the things they want. I am alarmed about this. Over one third of our gross national product today goes into taxes. The Minister of 23033-828

Finance must be as alarmed about this as I am. Where does it stop? We are not relieving the municipal taxpayer who still has to pay educational taxes amounting to half of his municipal taxes. Mr. Chairman, I shall not be very long. I cannot help rising when this new tax is imposed. My colleague, the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe) made a magnificent speech, and I support him fully when he objects to that new increase or to that new procedure of the government to get funds.
Be assured, Mr. Chairman, that we, in our party, are totally unable to support the government with regard to that legislation. We shall vote against it and we shall invite as many members as possible to object to such a procedure. We must denounce the misleading approach used by the government to impose again a new tax, and make the people believe that it is a gift for them. The legislation starts as follows:
That it is expedient to amend the Excise Tax Act to provide that, effective January 1, 1967, the rate of the consumption or sales tax imposed under section 30 of the said act be increased from 8 per cent to 9 per cent with respect to all goods subject to the said tax-
Now, Mr. Chairman, here in this expression "from 8 per cent to 9 per cent", it seems that the minister wants to soften the whipping that he is going to give once again to the poor taxpayer, to the small worker. The minister should tell him-at least, he should be frank -that the new tax of 1 per cent that he is imposing will actually increase the excise tax up to 12 per cent. Why not cease to play with words. From 8 per cent to 9 per cent? No, no. The tax actually stands at 11 per cent. Why does not the minister simply say that from now on, it will be 12 per cent, in order to

February 15, 1367
Ways and Means
show the people he is a little more frank, because when I hear such an announcement, I am wondering whether a minister can, in all seriousness, go back to the people without putting on at least a mask of sincerity.
That is partly what I do not like in practically all those pieces of legislation. On close study, one realizes that the final purpose of government measures is always to take more money from the taxpayers.
It is somewhat like fishing. The most attractive bait is put on the hook which is as small as possible to catch the whole thing. Successive governments have always proceeded in that manner. They weaken the worker, not enough to kill him but just enough to hold him and deprive him of any energy to revolt against governments.
Such is the rule of the game, because if the taxpayer becomes too strong, if he is given too much money and too much latitude, he would be very likely to revolt. Believe me, financiers secure in their position would not remain that way very long.
The people are weakened by taxes and their purchasing power is reduced all the time. Thus, it is possible to satisfy those who give orders.
Mind you, I am not criticizing the minister at all today. I duly noted his answer to the previous speaker who asked him whether he could not have found those $280 million elsewhere. The minister answered: there were only two things I could do, either borrow or impose a tax. Those were the only two methods, according to the minister: borrow or impose a tax.
I would have like the discussion to go on. because I understood the minister's words to mean that when a tax must be imposed, it always applies to the lower income groups.
I would like to hear the hon. minister say just for once if it would have been possible to get this money from those who can pay, the big financiers, whom he is constantly protecting, to whom he grants favours every day and who are permitted to have hidden reserves totalling two, three, four and five million dollars. We are told that there was no other alternative, that he was forced to introduce this tax. But to whom should it apply? We feel this tax should have been imposed on those who could pay.
I understand the hon. minister's position quite well. They could not act otherwise because they were elected precisely by those important financiers; they owe their seats to these people and they must watch over their

interests. It is well known that the two old parties are supported by financial interests. Someone was telling me the other day: "What can we do? They elected us, and we must work for them".
The minister is consistent. He was elected by financiers to protect them, to save them, to let them make money to the detriment of the people, as always and he fulfils his functions. What I do not like is when he tries to make the people believe that he is working in their best interest. This I like much less. Let him say it when he returns before the people: "I have fulfilled my function. I was elected by the financiers and I have worked on their behalf. If ever you want people to work for you, elect them. So far as I am concerned, I have worked for those who have elected me."
Well, Mr. Chairman, this is understandable, especially when it is realized how members of our group have been elected. They were elected with the pennies of the people, of the workers. We cannot put up with this sort of thing and that is why we insist on objecting. And we ask the people to open their eyes and to see how much they are being hoodwinked. If the people fail to open their eyes and if they keep on voting for these people every four years for $2, $3 or $5, I say that within two, three or four years, as the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac mentioned, in this democracy which is not a democracy at all but the worse monetary dictatorship ever in any country of the world, we will not hear anything more about private enterprise. To think that in our small towns the situation is such that certain businessmen are trying to sell their property because they are overtaxed.
There are municipal, school, provincial and federal taxes, and when all those taxes are paid, there is barely a livelihood left. And you have that 11 per cent tax on building materials which will increase by 1 per cent. If the government has no other means than to tax the worker, it should resign, for it has failed at its job.
It is undermining the foundations of this country in order to please a handful of big financiers. I believe the people will refuse to stand such a hoax any longer on thq part of financiers and especially of j governments which endlessly bait them in order to catch them and sell them to financiers.
Some of the older people will receive a maximum of $30; some others will get $20, $2, $3. In my area, a small group of people, about 15 per cent of the older people, will get a

little more. Perhaps more older people will get a larger amount in large centres, but in my area most of them are going to get something, namely $3, $4, $5. Now in order to be able to give $4, $5, $10 or $15 more to older people they are taxing everybody. Yes, everybody, except the rich. When I; say everybody, I mean the people as a whole. Great care is taken so that the rich will not be taxed. They are taxing the people as a whole, in order to give crumbs to older people, to provide bureaucrats with a handsome pay or to snoop around in the homes of our older people and then they will go proclaiming throughout the country: See, we gave you $30.
No, Mr. Chairman, I want to draw the people's attention to the fact that it is only a masquerade like most of the welfare legislation adopted here, and we strongly object to all that trickery practiced against the people.

I should also like to blame the government for forcing everybody to keep on working like hell in this prosperous country of ours. I should like to blame the government for not paying for all our medical, surgical and hospital services and for not paying for monthly vacations, check-ups and so on. I should like to blame the government for not bawling out the United States and telling them that we do not need any of their money in this prosperous country of ours. I should like to blame the government for not abolishing the taxes which are sucking the life blood out of all Canadians. I should like to blame the government for not changing this stupid natural law by which man is condemned to work by the sweat of his brow. In the first place, and this is quite interesting, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) mentioned earlier that the bill, even if it was quite simple, included four pages dealing with the sales tax and only one paragraph concerning old age security.
However, I wish to point out to him that three of the four pages he mentioned contain nothing but exceptions; in other words, these are items to which the new 1 per cent sales tax will not apply. Therefore, I was rather surprised at the intervention of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He said that the bill was very significant because it was four pages long, but had he taken the time to read the bill, he would have realized that three of the four pages he mentioned listed nothing but items exempt from the new sales tax.
The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), who also took part in the debate did not quite seem to understand the budget resolution. He accused the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) of not telling the truth and of not giving the house all the information available because the budget resolution mentions an increase in the sales tax from 8 to 9 per cent.
I should simply like to point out to him that this is, of course, a question of terminology, and that the Minister of Finance did not at any time mention that he was raising the sales tax from 11 to 12 per cent. The budget speech which he made on December 19, 1966 clearly indicated that the sales tax would be increased from 11 to 12 per cent, except in a few cases. He did not at any time try to misinform the house, and if the budget resolution mentioned an increase in the tax from 8 to 9 per cent, it was because the sales tax is divided into two different sectors, one added to the general revenue fund and the other to the old age security fund. But at no time did the minister imply that the sales tax was only of 9 per cent.
One of the most remarkable interjections, both on account of its brevity and its logic,
Excise Tax and Old Age Security Act was, I think, that of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain).
It is about time, Mr. Speaker, for the members of this house, who have been elected by the people, to start talking sense. It is useless to try to make people believe that we find money on trees or that some obscure mechanism in the Bank of Canada can be used to solve all our problems. Money spent at any level of government comes out of the pockets of the taxpayers.
I think that it is quite logical that we should be able to say to our electors that if we increased the old age security, we are ready to pay for it. It is no use postponing that tax increase for six, eight or 12 months; it would only be lying to the electors.
The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres was perfectly right when he said that too many in this house are trying to make believe that by passing legislation we could solve the problems very easily or that through a single piece of legislation we could guarantee a maximum income to all the taxpayers and citizens of Canada. The system is not like that; there is not a single system in the world which works like that. In any country, when an administration decides to grant social or other benefits to the population, it is because they have decided to raise taxes or get the money from the taxpayers' pockets.
This budget shows our concern not to direct taxes against people with small incomes. There is no clearer illustration of this than the raise in the old age security tax. We raised the maximum from $120 to $240. By so doing, we reached only one third of the taxpayers, those in the top income bracket, so that the other two thirds with lower incomes might not contribute at this time to the tax increase required to pay for the increased old age security.

However, due to the present state of our economy, we can not act irresponsibly. People expect more today, because they are better informed. Perhaps in 1910 or 1911, it was possible to get away with telling the people similar tales, but the information media being what they are today people are not easily taken in any more. I believe they can take their responsibilities and that is what we have been doing for several months.
It is interesting to note that last year, in the United States, newspapers and magazines were filled with articles criticizing the Johnson administration for refusing to accept its responsibilities, waiting until after the expected fall elections to raise the taxes. According to several economists, this delay caused excessive inflationary pressures throughout last spring and fall.
If the government had taken its responsibilities when the Canadian government did with the March 1966 budget, that is when we felt inflationary pressures in Canada; we took immediate action-the results would have been much better for the North American economy as a whole. And if Canada suffered from inflation during the last three months of 1966, it is perhaps mostly due to the fact that the Americans did not have the courage to act as the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) did here in Canada.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, after the minibudget was brought down the people said, as reported in the Canadian press: It is really painful and taxes are high, but there is a direct connection between government taxes and expenditures, and as the government had committed itself since March to maintain an almost balanced budget, there was nothing else to do than to levy a tax following the increase in old age security. And the advantage derived from this is that from now on, when we see electoral platforms, we might realize that there is a direct connection between the purse and the electoral program. And what is even more astonishing is that today we have heard, for the first time perhaps in 40 years in this house, the members of the New Democratic Party, for instance the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), say this: "It is true that the taxes should be raised when there is an increase in old age security."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when any minister of the crown comes into the house, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) did with this bill, and says that the bill is a simple one, that statement should serve as a red warning light to all members of the house to have a good look at the measure. I incline to the well-worn phrase, beware of Greeks bearing gifts.
Before dealing with the substance of the bill I wish to comment on its form. At the present time it seems that the Liberal government is showing a desire to lay all its eggs in one basket and then to scramble them thoroughly. I say this because yesterday the house concurred in a resolution preceding a money bill without any bill being introduced for first reading according to the normal procedure which we had expected would be followed. Now we find that we have before us a bill to amend two different acts.
There have been discussions in and outside the house among members about the desirability of moving toward a shortening of discussion on the resolution stage of bills. I suggest that if this trend continues we may find parliament faced one day with a situation where the government brings in all its resolutions at one time and at the end of the session introduces an omnibus bill with all the resolutions in one basket, so to speak. That would make it difficult indeed for members to determine what the principle of the bill was.
While what I have said so far may not be sufficient grounds for supporting the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), nevertheless there are substantial grounds for agreeing that this bill should not be read a second time now. The proposal to increase taxes is open to argument and arguments have already been advanced in that regard. The subject, it seems to me, divides itself into two parts. I can argue, as other members have, that the proposal to increase taxes at this time is unjustified and unwarranted. I propose to say,
Excise Tax and Old Age Security Act however, that if in the minister's view a tax increase at this time is necessary the minister has gone about imposing the increase in the wrong way.
I noticed that when my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis), was speaking, the canny Scottish instincts of the hon. member for Antigon-ish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) came to the fore. He raised the question of taxation and what we would propose to do. In that connection I say, not only about the proposal we have before us but also with respect to the levying of the federal sales tax in general, that I have long felt it is one of the most regressive forms of taxation in the country. Any proposal to increase such taxation should be resisted because it is regressive. Most of us know that this form of tax has a multiplier effect. The arguments advanced by hon. members such as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway about the unnecessary effect this tax has on the cost of living and its particular effect on the lower income groups are well justified.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: EXCISE TAX AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would he answer the question that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway declined to answer? Would he tell the house what kind of tax increase he would prefer if in the long run he is prepared to concede that a tax increase will be necessary?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
I am coming to that, and if the hon. member will be patient I will suggest something that he and the Minister of Finance might consider. I was about to say that under our marketing system mark-ups are made in percentages. Goods pass from the manufacturer to the wholesaler or jobber and then to the retail level, and the result is that the tax paid indirectly by the consumer is much greater than the amount flowing into the federal treasury as the result of the imposition of taxes. This is a wrong principle of taxation, I submit, and one which we should go to considerable lengths to avoid.
I am prepared to suggest something that the hon. member and the Minister of Finance might consider. We are all aware that between the federal and provincial levels of governments at various times these have been tax rental arrangements whereby the federal government has acted as the agent to collect taxes for remission to the provincial authorities. The Minister of Finance might consider asking for some quid pro quo in this connection. In other words, if at the federal level we

Excise Tax and Old Age Security Act collect taxes for the provincial authority, why should we not ask the provincial authority to do the same thing for us? If the Minister of Finance insists on using the sales tax approach to raise additional revenue I think it would be much less unfair to collect that tax at the retail level. Most of the provinces have arrangements for collecting sales tax and the people know how much they pay.
I offer this suggestion as my own idea. If the minister wants to discuss such a proposal at the next meeting of the federal and provincial finance ministers, and if he needs a 2 per cent sales tax increase, why could he not suggest to the provincial governments that instead of collecting 5 per cent they collect 7 per cent and remit the 2 per cent to the federal coffers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: Could I ask the hon. gentleman a question arising out of his interesting suggestion? Is he in favour of a sales tax?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: There is always an easy answer, of course, and that is to say that we do not like any taxes. However, we all recognize realities. I see the Minister of Finance applauding. One can say that the minister has a special reason for liking taxes less than some of the rest of us. We all agree that he has a duty to propose the levying of taxes in some form.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: What about a capital gains tax? There is lots of room there.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
As my leader suggests, a capital gains tax might be considered. That has been put forward from this quarter of the house many times. No minister of finance on the other side has ever seen fit to act on that suggestion. I am trying to suggest something a little different and I do so because, as I argued, the sales tax has a multiplier effect on the cost of goods at the retail level. It is a regressive form of taxation that we should seek to avoid and abolish.
On the general principle of having any sales tax there are arguments pro and con. If I entered into a discussion of that field I fear that Mr. Speaker might question whether my remarks were relevant to the principle of the bill before us. What I am prepared to argue is that a sales tax levied at the retail level is a much less unfair and, to that extent, more desirable form of taxation than the proposition the minister has put forward in this bill.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: I was moved to rise by the remarks of the parliamentary secretary, which I found to be both amusing and confusing. First of all, we object to any increase in the sales tax because we know from experience that an increase of 1 per cent amounts to a great deal more when it is passed on to the consumer. subtopic: EXCISE TAX AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
I come from the province of Manitoba where only last week the Conservative provincial government introduced a sales tax. The provincial governments, whatever party they may represent, have found to their sorrow that the sales tax is one of the few sources from which they can raise revenue. I do not like it and they do not like it. I am suggesting that the federal government has a great deal more flexibility and that no federal government needs to increase a sales tax which is already too high.
In the few moments at my disposal I should like to deal with the rhetorical question asked by the parliamentary secretary. He knew the answer before he asked it. There are a number of ways in which the Minister of Finance could have raised the money he thought he needed to pay for the increases which will go

to the old age pensioners. Several members have already mentioned a capital gains tax. We have also suggested that the $1.5 billion being spent on national defence could be reduced substantially without greatly impairing the efficiency of our defence forces.
I wish to deal specifically, however, with one clause in the bill under which I suggest the minister might have raised a very substantial amount of money. I refer to the proposal in clause 5 under which the act is amended so that 4 per cent of a taxpayer's taxable income for the year is earmarked for his old age security contribution up to a maximum of $240 a year. I made a rough calculation to see how this affects me personally. I found that if there were no limitation of $240 I would be paying $360 or another 50 per cent. I suggest to the minister that members of parliament, cabinet ministers, who make even more money than ordinary members, and the business and professional people of this country who make $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 a year or more can afford to pay 4 per cent without a maximum of $240 a great deal more easily than the hundreds of thousands who will find that as a result of the sales tax the cost of every item they buy has been increased, save for the few exceptions listed in the bill.
Why has the minister not seen fit to abolish this limitation? He has not done so for a very simple reason. He believes it is wrong for the rich to pay much more than they will get from the pension when they receive it. There can be no other explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: The hon. member is attributing motives to me which I deny most forcefully. The reason I have done this is to follow the pattern which he and his party have endorsed over many years. The amount of the limiting figure has been increased in a series of steps-$90, $120, $240. I deny the implication that I am following my present course in order to protect anybody in the community.
